title: Capstone: A Health Question and the Evidence
bigQuestion: How can you answer a health question fairly, using the best evidence from every tradition?

story.title: Grandma's Honey and a Fair Test
story.kicker: A student sets out to prove her grandmother's cough remedy works, and learns to design a fair test instead.
paragraphs: Every winter, when Nadia coughed at night, her grandmother warmed a spoonful of honey with lemon and sat on the edge of the bed until she swallowed it. Her grandmother had learned it from her own mother in Lebanon. The cough always seemed to calm down. So when her health teacher assigned a capstone project, Nadia knew her topic right away. She would prove that Grandma's honey works.

Her teacher, Mr. Okafor, liked the question. Then he asked one of his own. "How would you know the cough did not calm down by itself?" Coughs from colds get better on their own over days. Nadia also always felt comforted when her grandmother sat with her. Was it the honey, the time, or the love? Nadia realized that her memories could not separate those things.

So she changed her goal. Instead of proving the remedy, she would find out what fair tests had shown. She learned that a fair test compares groups. One group gets honey. Another gets nothing, or a look-alike, or a common cough medicine. Families are assigned to groups by chance. Then researchers count coughs the same way in every group.

Then she found a Cochrane review, a careful summary of many such trials. It reported that honey may ease children's cough symptoms somewhat better than no treatment, though the studies were small. It also carried a firm safety rule that her grandmother had not known: never give honey to a baby under one year old. Nadia's final project honored her grandmother, told the truth about the evidence, and taught her family something new.
story.think: Nadia started out wanting to prove something. Why did she end up with a stronger project by trying to test it fairly instead?

lessons.title: Choosing Your Question
lessons.mainIdea: A strong capstone question is about something you care about, can be answered with evidence, and is narrow enough to study.
reading: Look at three possible questions. Does tai chi prevent falls in older adults? How did Bangladesh reduce deaths of young children? Should health insurance cover acupuncture for back pain? Each one names a real situation, and each can be studied with published evidence. That makes each a good *research question*: a clear question that evidence can help answer.

Some questions are too big. "Is traditional medicine good?" covers thousands of practices and cannot be answered in one project. Narrow it by naming who, what and which result. "Does tai chi reduce falls in adults over 65?" is focused. Some questions are about facts, and some are about values. "Should insurance cover it?" needs facts about benefit and cost, and also a judgment about fairness.

Start with something that matters to you: a family remedy, a sport injury, a news story, or a health gap in your community. Write the question in one sentence. Then ask three things. Can I find reliable evidence on it? Is it narrow enough? Could the answer surprise me? If the answer to the last one is no, you may be trying to prove something rather than find out.

words.d: a clear, focused question that evidence can help answer
limited to a specific group, treatment and result so it can be studied well
a question about what should be done, which needs both facts and a judgment about what matters

look.title: Sharpen the Question
look.text: First draft: "Is ginger good for you?" Second draft: "Does ginger help nausea?" Third draft: "Does ginger reduce nausea in pregnant women, compared with no treatment?" Each draft names more clearly who is helped, what is given and what result is measured.
look.prompt: Write your own first-draft health question. Then sharpen it twice, the way the ginger question was sharpened.

check.q: Why is "Is traditional medicine good?" a weak capstone question?
choices: It is too broad to answer in one project
It is about a value only
check.why: The lesson says it covers thousands of practices and cannot be answered in one project.

check.q: Which question is both about facts and about values?
choices: How many people are over 65 in Illinois?
Should insurance cover acupuncture for back pain?
check.why: A should question needs facts about benefit and cost and a judgment about fairness.

check.q: What warning sign does the lesson give about your question?
choices: It uses the word tai chi
The answer could never surprise you
check.why: If no answer could surprise you, you may be trying to prove something rather than find out.

lessons.title: Four Parts of a Clear Question
lessons.mainIdea: Clinical questions are often built from four parts: the people, the treatment, the comparison and the outcome.
reading: Doctors who search for evidence often use a pattern called *PICO*. P is the population, the people the question is about. I is the intervention, the treatment or action being tested. C is the comparison, what it is measured against. O is the outcome, the result that matters. Writing each part down turns a vague idea into a searchable question.

Try it on falls. P: adults over 65 living at home. I: a tai chi class twice a week. C: no class, or a different kind of exercise. O: the number of falls in a year. Now the question reads, "In adults over 65, does twice-weekly tai chi reduce falls compared with no class?" Those words are also the search terms you will type into a database.

The *outcome* deserves the most thought. A study might show that tai chi improves balance on a lab test. That is useful, but the result that matters most to an older person is not falling and staying independent. Look for studies that measure outcomes people actually care about, such as falls, pain, days of school missed or survival.

words.d: a way to build a clinical question: population, intervention, comparison and outcome
the treatment or action being tested in a study
the result a study measures, such as falls, pain or survival
what a treatment is measured against, such as no treatment or another treatment

look.title: Fill In the Parts
look.text: Nadia's question: "In children aged 1 to 12 with a cough from a cold, does a spoonful of honey at bedtime reduce how often they cough at night, compared with no treatment?"
look.prompt: Label the P, the I, the C and the O in Nadia's question. Which part do you think is hardest to measure well, and why?

check.q: In PICO, what does the C stand for?
check.why: C is the comparison: what the treatment is measured against.

check.q: In the tai chi example, which is the outcome?
choices: The number of falls in a year
check.why: The outcome is the result measured, here the number of falls.

check.q: Why does the lesson say the outcome deserves the most thought?
choices: Because it should measure what matters to people, like falls, not only lab scores
Because outcomes are always easy to count
Because the outcome is the same as the population
check.why: The lesson urges looking for outcomes people care about, such as falls or pain.

lessons.title: Not All Evidence Is Equal
lessons.mainIdea: Systematic reviews of well-designed trials usually give stronger evidence than single studies, expert opinion or personal stories.
reading: Nadia's grandmother's story is a kind of evidence, called an *anecdote*: one person's experience. Anecdotes matter. They often start good questions. But they cannot tell whether a result came from the remedy, from time, or from chance. Stronger kinds of evidence are designed to separate those causes.

A *randomized controlled trial*, or RCT, assigns people by chance to a treatment group or a comparison group and then compares outcomes. Because chance decides who gets what, the groups start out alike. An *observational study* watches what people already do, such as comparing people who drink green tea with people who do not. It can find links, but people who choose green tea may differ in other ways too.

A *systematic review* gathers every good study on one question, judges their quality, and often combines their results. The Cochrane Collaboration, founded in 1993, is a well-known group that publishes such reviews. For most treatment questions, a recent systematic review of RCTs is the strongest place to start. Some questions, such as rare side effects, depend more on large observational studies.

words.d: a story of one person's experience; useful for ideas but weak as proof
a study that assigns people by chance to a treatment or a comparison group
a study that watches what people already do, without assigning a treatment
a careful summary that gathers and judges all good studies on one question

look.title: Rank the Evidence
look.text: Four sources on whether a vitamin prevents colds: (A) a celebrity says it keeps her healthy. (B) A survey finds that people who take it report fewer colds. (C) One trial randomly assigns 300 students to the vitamin or a look-alike pill. (D) A review combines 25 such trials with 11,000 people.
look.prompt: Rank A to D from weakest to strongest evidence. Explain why B could show a link even if the vitamin does nothing.

check.q: What makes a randomized controlled trial strong?
choices: Chance decides who gets the treatment, so the groups start out alike
It lasts at least ten years
check.why: Random assignment makes the groups similar, so differences in outcome can be traced to the treatment.

check.q: Why can an observational study of green tea drinkers mislead?
choices: The study is always too small
People who choose green tea may differ in other ways too
check.why: Observational studies find links, but the groups may differ in other ways besides the tea.

check.q: What does a systematic review do?
choices: Tests a drug in animals only
Gathers and judges all good studies on one question
check.why: A systematic review gathers every good study on a question, judges quality and often combines results.

lessons.title: Trusted Places to Look
lessons.mainIdea: Public health agencies, research institutes and peer-reviewed journals are reliable starting points for health evidence.
reading: When you search a health question online, the first results may be ads or sellers. Start instead with trusted bodies. The *World Health Organization* (WHO) sets global guidance. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) tracks disease and publishes prevention advice. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) funds and reports medical research.

For traditional and complementary practices, the NIH's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, or NCCIH, publishes plain-language pages. They cover acupuncture, tai chi, yoga, herbs and more. Each page says what the tradition teaches, what research has found, and what safety concerns exist. PubMed, a free database from the National Library of Medicine, lists millions of research articles and lets you filter for systematic reviews.

Many research articles are *peer-reviewed*. That means other experts read the study before publication and asked for fixes. Peer review catches many errors, but not all, so one study is never the final word. Also note the date. A 2024 review may include trials that a 2010 page never saw. Write down every source's author or body, title and year as you go.

words.d: checked by other experts in the field before being published
a free database from the U.S. National Library of Medicine that lists research articles
the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, part of NIH, which studies traditional and complementary practices
the United Nations agency that leads on global health

look.title: Tell Your Care Team
look.text: The NCCIH advises people to tell all of their health care providers about any complementary or integrative approaches they use, including herbs and supplements. Giving a full picture helps keep care coordinated and safe.
look.cite: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, NIH, "Be an Informed Consumer" guidance (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why might a pharmacist need to know that a patient drinks an herbal tea every day? Connect your answer to what you learned about medicines in this course.

check.q: Which source is a good starting point for evidence on tai chi or herbs?
choices: The NCCIH pages from the NIH
A company that sells the herb
check.why: The NCCIH publishes plain pages on complementary practices, including research findings and safety.

check.q: What does peer-reviewed mean?
choices: Checked by other experts before publication
check.why: Peer review means other experts read and questioned the study before it was published; it catches many errors but not all.

check.q: Why does the lesson say to note each source's date?
choices: A newer review may include trials an older page never saw
Only sources from this year count
check.why: Newer reviews can include newer trials, so the date affects how complete the evidence is.

lessons.title: Spotting Weak Claims
lessons.mainIdea: Watch for red flags, such as miracle promises, hidden sellers and no named evidence, whether a claim is about a modern or a traditional treatment.
reading: A website says a tea "cures diabetes naturally in 30 days" and "doctors don't want you to know." A second site sells a new pill with a smiling scientist and a chart with no labels. Both show *red flags*: signs that a health claim may not be trustworthy. Red flags can show up for modern products and for traditional ones alike.

Common red flags include promises to cure serious diseases, claims that one product fixes many unrelated problems, stories instead of studies, and warnings not to trust your doctor. Ask who made the page and whether they profit. That is a *conflict of interest*: a reason someone might favor a result, such as selling the product. Studies should disclose conflicts, and readers should notice them.

Checking a claim does not mean mocking it. Many traditional remedies have been studied fairly, with mixed results. The goal is to ask the same fair questions of every claim: What is the evidence? Who says so? How strong is it? If a claim involves a serious illness, talk with a doctor, nurse or pharmacist before changing any treatment.

words.d: a warning sign that a claim may not be trustworthy
a reason, such as making money, that might lead someone to favor a result
a statement that something is true, which should be backed by evidence

look.title: Two Labels
look.text: Label 1: "Ancient formula! Cures arthritis, anxiety and cancer. No side effects!" Label 2: "This tea is traditionally used for mild stomach upset. Research is limited. Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or take other medicines."
look.prompt: List the red flags on Label 1. What makes Label 2 more honest, even though it is less exciting?

check.q: Which is a red flag in a health claim?
choices: The page names its studies and their dates
The page promises to cure a serious disease quickly
The page suggests talking to a pharmacist
The page says research is limited
check.why: Promises to cure serious diseases are one of the red flags listed in the lesson.

check.q: A study praising a supplement was paid for by the company that sells it. What is this?
check.why: A conflict of interest is a reason, like profit, that might lead someone to favor a result.

check.q: According to the lesson, how should traditional and modern claims be checked?
choices: Ask the same fair questions of every claim
check.why: The lesson says to ask the same fair questions about evidence of every claim, without mocking.

lessons.title: What Makes a Test Fair
lessons.mainIdea: Fair tests use a comparison group, assign people by chance, and when possible keep people from knowing who got which treatment.
reading: In 1747, aboard the British ship HMS Salisbury, the Scottish surgeon James Lind cared for sailors sick with scurvy. He chose twelve with similar symptoms and gave pairs of them different added foods or drinks, such as cider, vinegar, seawater, or oranges and lemons. The pair given citrus fruit recovered fastest. Lind's small study is often called one of the first controlled trials, because he compared groups side by side.

Modern fair tests add more. A *control group* gets no treatment, a usual treatment or a *placebo*, a look-alike with no active ingredient. Random assignment decides who goes where. *Blinding* means patients, and often the researchers, do not know who got the real treatment. That matters because expecting to feel better can change how people feel and how researchers judge results.

Some treatments are hard to blind. You cannot hide from someone that they are doing tai chi. Researchers then compare tai chi with another activity, such as stretching, and use judges who do not know the groups to count the outcome. For acupuncture, some trials use a sham, such as needles placed at points the tradition does not use, and the choice of sham itself is debated.

words.d: the group in a study that does not get the treatment being tested, used for comparison
a look-alike treatment with no active ingredient, used as a comparison
keeping patients, and often researchers, from knowing who got which treatment
a fake version of a procedure, used as a comparison in trials of treatments like acupuncture

look.title: Lind's Result
look.text: Lind reported that the most sudden and visible good effects came from the oranges and lemons. One of the two sailors given them was fit for duty within about six days, and the other was well enough to help nurse the rest.
look.cite: James Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy, 1753 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Lind had only two sailors per group and no blinding. Name one way his test was fair and one way a modern trial would make it stronger.

check.q: Why is James Lind's 1747 scurvy study remembered?
choices: It was the first vaccine trial
It compared groups side by side, like an early controlled trial
check.why: Lind gave different groups different treatments and compared them, an early controlled trial.

check.q: What is a placebo?
choices: A look-alike with no active ingredient
check.why: A placebo looks like the real treatment but has no active ingredient.

check.q: Why do researchers use blinding?
choices: Because expecting to feel better can change results
check.why: Expectations can change how people feel and how results are judged, so blinding hides who got what.

lessons.title: Case Study: Tai Chi and Falls
lessons.mainIdea: Tai chi comes from Chinese martial and health traditions, and trials suggest it can reduce falls in older adults.
reading: In a park in Chicago's Chinatown, a group of older adults moves slowly together through a set of flowing steps. This is *tai chi*, a practice that grew from Chinese martial arts. In Traditional Chinese Medicine, tai chi is understood to help the smooth flow of qi, the tradition's idea of vital energy, while calming the mind and building balance.

Falls are a leading cause of injury for older adults, so researchers have tested whether exercise can help. A 2019 Cochrane systematic review by Catherine Sherrington and colleagues gathered trials of exercise for older people living in the community. It found that balance and functional exercise reduces the rate of falls, and that tai chi may reduce it too, though the evidence for tai chi was less certain.

Notice how two views fit together here. Science does not measure qi, so it cannot confirm the tradition's explanation. But it can measure falls, and on that outcome the evidence is encouraging. The CDC includes tai chi-based balance programs among options to help prevent falls. A fair capstone would state both points clearly and respectfully.

words.d: a slow, flowing movement practice that grew from Chinese martial arts
in Traditional Chinese Medicine, the idea of a vital energy that flows through the body
how many falls happen in a group over a set time

look.title: Two Kinds of Claims
look.text: Claim A: "Tai chi improves the flow of qi." Claim B: "Older adults who take tai chi classes fall less often than those who do not." One claim comes from inside a tradition. The other can be counted in a trial.
look.prompt: Which claim can a randomized trial test directly? How would you write about the other claim respectfully in your capstone?

check.q: What did the 2019 Cochrane review find about exercise and falls?
choices: Balance exercise reduces the rate of falls, and tai chi may too
check.why: The review found balance and functional exercise reduces falls, with tai chi possibly helping but less certain.

check.q: In Traditional Chinese Medicine, what is qi?
choices: The tradition's idea of a vital energy that flows through the body
check.why: Qi is named in the lesson as the tradition's idea of vital energy, not a measured fact.

check.q: What can science measure in the tai chi question?
check.why: The lesson says science cannot measure qi but can measure outcomes such as falls.

lessons.title: Case Study: Saving Children's Lives
lessons.mainIdea: Deaths of children under five fell by more than half worldwide since 1990, thanks to many simple, tested public-health steps.
reading: In Bangladesh in the 1980s, health workers went village to village teaching families to mix clean water, sugar and salt. This is *oral rehydration solution*, or ORS. Diarrhea can drain water and salt from a child's body quickly, and ORS replaces them. Trials in Bangladesh and India helped show it works, and it became one of the most important child-health tools in the world.

Worldwide, the number of children who die before age five has fallen sharply. The UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation reports about 12.8 million such deaths in 1990 and about 4.9 million in 2022, even as the world's population grew. The *under-five mortality rate*, deaths per 1,000 live births, fell by more than half.

No single cure did this. Vaccines, ORS, bed nets against malaria, clean water, skilled birth attendants, better nutrition and girls' education all played parts. Many of these steps were tested in trials and scaled up by governments and community health workers. A capstone on this question would compare several causes and ask which evidence is strongest for each.

words.d: a drink of clean water, sugar and salt that replaces fluids lost from diarrhea
the number of children who die before age five for every 1,000 born alive
a trained local person who brings basic health care and teaching to neighbors

look.title: Deaths of Children Under Five, Worldwide
look.cite: UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (UN IGME), Levels and Trends in Child Mortality, report 2023
look.prompt: By about how much did yearly deaths of young children fall from 1990 to 2022? Name two causes from the lesson that you would research.

check.q: What does oral rehydration solution do?
choices: Replaces water and salt lost from diarrhea
check.why: ORS is clean water, sugar and salt that replaces fluids lost in diarrhea.

check.q: About how many children died before age five in 2022, according to UN estimates?
check.why: The UN IGME estimate given in the lesson is about 4.9 million in 2022, down from 12.8 million in 1990.

check.q: What does the lesson say caused the drop in child deaths?
choices: Many tested steps, such as vaccines, ORS, bed nets and clean water
check.why: The lesson says no single cure did it; many tested steps worked together.

lessons.title: Known, Unknown, Concluded
lessons.mainIdea: A strong conclusion separates what the evidence shows, what is still unknown, and what you conclude and why.
reading: Nadia's final page had three headings. Under *What is known*, she wrote that a Cochrane review found honey may ease children's cough symptoms more than no treatment, and that honey must never be given to babies under one. Under *What is not known*, she wrote that the trials were small and short. Under *My conclusion*, she said honey is a reasonable, low-cost comfort for coughs in children over one, while serious or lasting coughs need a doctor.

This structure keeps you honest. The *certainty* of evidence describes how sure we can be that a result is true. Cochrane and many guideline groups rate certainty as high, moderate, low or very low. Use their words. "May help" fits low certainty; "helps" fits high certainty. Never make a finding sound stronger than the evidence.

Where a question is contested, describe the main views fairly. For example, experts disagree about whether acupuncture's benefits for some kinds of back pain come from the needling itself or from the care and expectation around it. Say that. Then state your own conclusion, with your reasons, and say what new evidence would change your mind.

words.d: how sure we can be that a research finding is true, often rated high, moderate, low or very low
your final answer to the question, with reasons drawn from the evidence
argued about by experts, with more than one reasonable view

look.title: Match the Words to the Evidence
look.text: Three findings: (1) Many large trials show a vaccine prevents a disease: high certainty. (2) A few small trials suggest an herb eases mild anxiety: low certainty. (3) One tiny study hints a diet helps memory: very low certainty.
look.prompt: Write one honest sentence about each finding, choosing words like "clearly helps," "may help" or "we do not know yet."

check.q: Which wording fits low-certainty evidence?
check.why: The lesson says "may help" fits low certainty; never make a finding sound stronger than the evidence.

check.q: What belongs under What is not known in Nadia's project?
choices: Honey should not be given to babies
The trials were small and short
check.why: Nadia listed the small, short trials as a limit of what is known.

check.q: When a question is contested, what should your capstone do?
choices: Pick one side and hide the other
Describe the main views fairly, then give your conclusion and reasons
check.why: The lesson says to describe the main views fairly, then state your conclusion and what would change your mind.

lessons.title: Presenting With Respect
lessons.mainIdea: Present your findings clearly, cite every source, and speak about every tradition and every person with respect.
reading: Imagine presenting to a class where one classmate's family uses Ayurvedic remedies, another's uses traditional Mexican herbal teas, and another's relies on a hospital for a long illness. Everyone in the room has reasons for their choices. A respectful presentation names each tradition in its own terms, such as "Ayurveda teaches…", and then reports the evidence plainly.

Keep the audience in mind. Use a clear question on your first slide, a few key findings, and one simple chart or table. Define any hard word. Put a *citation* for every fact: who said it, what the source is called, and the year. If you quote someone, use their exact words and mark them; otherwise *paraphrase*, which means restating an idea in your own words while still naming the source.

End with care. Remind listeners that your project is not medical advice. Anyone thinking about a treatment should talk with a doctor, nurse or pharmacist, and should tell them about any herbs or supplements. Then invite questions, and listen. A good health presentation leaves people better informed, and still feeling respected.

words.d: a note that tells who wrote a source, what it is called and when it was published
to restate an idea in your own words while still naming where it came from
the people who will read or hear your work

look.title: Two Opening Lines
look.text: Opening A: "Old remedies are just superstition, and I will show you why." Opening B: "Many families, including mine, use honey for coughs. I wanted to know what fair tests have found."
look.prompt: How might different classmates feel hearing each opening? Rewrite Opening A so it is respectful and still honest.

check.q: What is a respectful way to describe a traditional practice?
choices: Name it in its own terms, such as "Ayurveda teaches," then report the evidence
check.why: The lesson says to name each tradition in its own terms, then report the evidence plainly.

check.q: What should a citation include?
choices: Who wrote it, the title and the year
check.why: A citation tells who wrote the source, what it is called and when it was published.

check.q: Why should a capstone end by pointing listeners to a doctor, nurse or pharmacist?
choices: Because students may not present health topics
Because the project is not medical advice
Because the audience must buy medicine
check.why: The lesson reminds presenters that their project is not medical advice, so treatment choices need a professional.

review.q: Why did Nadia change her goal from proving the honey remedy to testing it fairly?
choices: Her memories could not separate the honey from time and comfort
Honey is not a real remedy
She found no sources at all
review.why: Colds improve on their own and her grandmother's care comforted her, so memories alone could not show the honey's effect.

review.q: In PICO, which part is "twice-weekly tai chi classes"?
review.why: The intervention is the treatment or action being tested.

review.q: Which evidence is usually strongest for a treatment question?
choices: A recent systematic review of randomized trials
review.why: The lesson says a recent systematic review of RCTs is usually the strongest place to start.

review.q: Which of these is a trusted starting point for health evidence?
choices: An ad in a search result
review.why: The CDC is a public health agency that tracks disease and publishes prevention advice.

review.q: What made James Lind's scurvy study an early fair test?
choices: He compared several groups given different treatments
He gave everyone the same food
review.why: Lind compared pairs of sailors given different treatments side by side.

review.q: How does the tai chi case show Western and traditional views side by side?
choices: Trials show tai chi causes falls
Science cannot measure qi but can measure falls, where results are encouraging
review.why: The lesson says science cannot confirm qi but can count falls, and the evidence there is encouraging.

review.q: Which step helped reduce deaths of young children worldwide?
review.why: ORS, along with vaccines, bed nets and clean water, helped cut child deaths.

review.q: A few small trials suggest a remedy helps. Which sentence reports this honestly?
choices: It may help, but the evidence is limited
review.why: Low-certainty evidence fits wording like "may help," with the limits stated.
